--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.add_paley_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Add the Paley graph of a prime p: numbers modulo p joined when they differ by a twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.add_paley_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Add the Paley graph of a prime p: numbers modulo p joined when they differ by a title: >- [Graph.add_paley_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Add the Paley graph of a prime p: numbers modulo p joined when they differ by a page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Add the Paley graph of a prime `p`: numbers modulo `p` joined when they differ by a ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L19673-L19815){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.add_paley_graph( p, type=None, label=True, rel=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} square. ![Paley graph](../assets/graphs/add-paley-graph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Three Paley graphs on the integers modulo a prime p, on a ring. At p=5 two numbers are joined when their difference is a nonzero square, 1 or 4, which gives a five-cycle. At p=3 and p=7, where -1 is not a square, the graph is directed: each pair gets exactly one arc, from x to x plus a nonzero square, making a tournament, a directed triangle at p=3 and 21 arcs at p=7." width="100%"} Creates `p` nodes `0, 1, ..., p - 1` and joins `x` to `x + s mod p` for every nonzero square `s` modulo `p` (the quadratic residues, of which a prime has `(p - 1) / 2`). When `p = 1 mod 4`, `-1` is a square, so the relation is symmetric and the Paley graph is an undirected, `(p - 1) / 2`-regular, strongly regular graph that is isomorphic to its own complement; Paley graphs are standard examples of pseudo-random graphs with excellent expansion. When `p = 3 mod 4`, exactly one of `x - y` and `y - x` is a square, and the directed version is the Paley tournament. In a directed graph every relation `x -> x + s` becomes an edge, as in NetworkX's `paley_graph()` (which returns a directed graph): for `p = 1 mod 4` each pair is joined in both directions. In an undirected graph each related pair gets a single edge, from the earlier-created node to the later one, so `p = 3 mod 4` gives a complete graph. `p` is not checked for primality. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Paley graphs are useful for: - strongly regular and self-complementary examples, with known spectra - pseudo-random graphs that behave like `G(p, 1/2)` but are fully deterministic - Paley tournaments, which are standard examples in tournament theory and Ramsey theory ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [p]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes, normally a prime. Must be non-negative. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `p=` is negative. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~complement`) : Return the complement, which a Paley graph is isomorphic to. [](`~add_chordal_cycle_graph`) : Build an expander from inverses modulo a prime. [](`~is_regular_expander`) : Check the spectral expansion of a regular graph. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The Paley graph of 13 joins two numbers when their difference is a square modulo `13`. It's 6-regular and isomorphic to its own complement: ::: {#a9b9ad31 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_paley_graph(p=13) degrees = set(graph.degrees(return_dict=True).values()) graph.count_edges(), degrees, graph.is_isomorphic(graph.complement()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (39, {6}, True) ``` ::: ::: The Paley graph of 5 is the 5-cycle: ::: {#e1a1087c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} pentagon = ec.Graph().add_paley_graph(p=5) pentagon.is_isomorphic(ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: ::: For `p = 7` the directed version is a tournament: all `7 * 6 / 2 = 21` pairs are joined exactly once, and every node beats three others: ::: {#62ad4a79 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} tournament = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_paley_graph(p=7) nodes = tournament.get_node_ids() wins = [len(tournament.get_neighbors(v)) for v in nodes] tournament.count_edges(), wins ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (21, [3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3]) ``` ::: ::: ### The graph and its complement The Paley graph of 13 on the left and its complement on the right, with the nodes in order around a circle. The squares modulo `13` are `1, 3, 4, 9, 10, 12`, so on the left each node is joined to the nodes `1`, `3` and `4` steps away; the complement takes the other steps, `2`, `5` and `6`. The drawings differ, but doubling every number modulo `13` turns one into the other: ::: {#0d86d791 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} complement = graph.complement() neighbors = graph.get_neighbors("1") sorted(int(graph.get_label_from_id(n)) - 1 for n in neighbors) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [1, 3, 4, 9, 10, 12] ``` ::: ::: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#e21dd13e .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.layout_circular(order="id").plot( layout="pos", label_by="label", width=320, height=320, legend=False ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
